title: Catecholamine-Induced Dysregulation of Cardiac Developmental Regulators in Pheochromocytoma-Associated Cardiomyopathy: A Systematic Review with Clinical Implications for Cardiac Remodeling
content: Objective: This study aims to investigate how chronic catecholamine excess in pheochromocytoma dysregulates cardiac developmental regulators, and to assess its clinical implications for cardiomyocyte fate instability, maladaptive cardiac remodeling, disease progression, risk assessment, and identification of potential targets for early diagnosis and therapeutic intervention in pheochromocytoma-associated cardiomyopathy. Background: Pheochromocytoma causes sustained catecholamine excess leading to cardiomyopathy that is not fully explained by acute toxicity or hemodynamic stress. Emerging evidence suggests chronic beta-adrenergic stimulation may induce epigenetic and transcriptional reprogramming in cardiomyocytes, involving developmental regulators such as ISL1, NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, MEF2C, HAND1/2, MYOCD, MSX2, HOPX, and pathways including Wnt, Notch, FGF, and BMP. Clinically, this may explain variable recovery and persistent dysfunction after tumor treatment. Methods: Databases, including PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through April 2026, to investigate how catecholamines released in pheochromocytoma disrupt cardiomyocyte cell-type specific programming by targeting key cardiac developmental genes, transcription factors and signaling pathways, leading to pheochromocytoma-associated cardiomyopathy, and its implications for cardiac remodeling and clinical outcomes. Studies meeting the criteria outlined in the methods section were systematically reviewed to address the research question. This study adheres to the relevant PRISMA 2020 (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. Results: Sustained catecholamine excess in Pheochromocytoma induces widespread transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming in cardiomyocytes, leading to dysregulation of key developmental gene networks including ISL1, NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, MEF2C, HAND1/2, MYOCD, MSX2, and HOPX, along with Wnt, Notch, FGF, and BMP pathways. This results in partial reactivation of embryonic programs, cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation, and transcriptional instability. These changes impair contractile function and promote fibrosis, structural disorganization, and electrical instability, collectively driving maladaptive cardiac remodeling and contributing to the pathogenesis of catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy. This has profound clinical implications for cardiac remodeling. Conclusion: Catecholamine excess in pheochromocytoma reveals a novel paradigm in which neurohormonal stress reactivates embryonic cardiac gene networks through epigenetic remodeling rather than solely causing toxic injury. This process induces partial developmental reprogramming of cardiomyocytes, disrupting lineage stability and producing a hybrid fetal-adult transcriptional state. Key pathways including Wnt, Notch, FGF, and BMP become aberrantly engaged, driving transcriptional incoherence and functional decline. The resulting maladaptive remodeling reframes cardiomyopathy as a failure of developmental silencing mechanisms, linking endocrine stress to persistent cardiomyocyte fate instability and structural cardiac reorganization.
